title: The Character Table of $S_4$
---

:::lede
With the results of Chapter 13 we can compute the character table of a given group without first constructing all of its representations. We use the notation of that chapter: $V_1, \ldots, V_k$ are the irreducible representations of $G$, $\chi_i$ their characters, and $H$ the inner product on class functions (Definition [13.5.3](/notes/math-55a/13-5-orthogonality-of-characters#definition-13-5-3)). The tools are these.

- The number of irreducible representations equals the number of conjugacy classes (Theorem [13.6.2](/notes/math-55a/13-6-characters-form-an-orthonormal-basis#theorem-13-6-2)), and the squares of their dimensions add up to $|G|$ (Corollary [13.5.11](/notes/math-55a/13-5-orthogonality-of-characters#corollary-13-5-11)).
- The irreducible characters are orthonormal (Theorem [13.5.4](/notes/math-55a/13-5-orthogonality-of-characters#theorem-13-5-4)), and the columns of the table are orthogonal (Proposition [13.6.5](/notes/math-55a/13-6-characters-form-an-orthonormal-basis#proposition-13-6-5)).
- A representation $W$ is irreducible exactly when $H(\chi_W, \chi_W) = 1$ (Corollary [13.5.7](/notes/math-55a/13-5-orthogonality-of-characters#corollary-13-5-7)), and $H(\chi_i, \chi_W)$ is the multiplicity of $V_i$ in $W$ (Corollary [13.5.6](/notes/math-55a/13-5-orthogonality-of-characters#corollary-13-5-6)).
- New representations come from old ones: permutation representations, twists by $1$-dimensional representations (Proposition [13.5.8](/notes/math-55a/13-5-orthogonality-of-characters#proposition-13-5-8)), tensor products, symmetric and exterior squares, whose characters are given by Proposition [13.4.3](/notes/math-55a/13-4-characters#proposition-13-4-3).

We work out the character tables of $S_4$, $A_4$, $S_5$ and $A_5$ in this way; the table of $S_3$ is Example [13.4.5](/notes/math-55a/13-4-characters#example-13-4-5). The chapter ends with the representation ring, which packages the operations $\oplus$ and $\otimes$ into a ring.

For a symmetric group, $U$, $U'$ and $V$ denote its trivial, alternating and standard representations (Example [13.1.4](/notes/math-55a/13-1-representations-and-subrepresentations#example-13-1-4)), and $\chi_V(\sigma) = |\{i : \sigma(i) = i\}| - 1$, because $U \oplus V$ is the permutation representation, whose character counts fixed points. In the tables, each column is labelled by a representative of a conjugacy class, with the size of the class below it. When we write a class function as a vector, its entries are its values on the classes in the order of the table.

Two general facts about $1$-dimensional representations will be used repeatedly. First, if $L$ is $1$-dimensional and $X$ is irreducible, then $X \otimes L$ is irreducible with character $\chi_X\chi_L$ (Proposition [13.5.8](/notes/math-55a/13-5-orthogonality-of-characters#proposition-13-5-8)). Second, $S_n$ ($n \geq 2$) has exactly two $1$-dimensional representations, $U$ and $U'$. Indeed, a homomorphism $\theta : S_n \to \CC^*$ takes the same value $c$ on all transpositions, since they are conjugate (Theorem [3.4.6](/notes/math-55a/3-4-the-symmetric-group#theorem-3-4-6)) and $\CC^*$ is abelian; and $c^2 = \theta(e) = 1$. As the transpositions generate $S_n$ (Proposition [3.4.9](/notes/math-55a/3-4-the-symmetric-group#proposition-3-4-9)), $\theta$ is the constant function $1$ if $c = 1$, and $\theta = \sgn$ if $c = -1$.
:::

By Theorem [3.4.6](/notes/math-55a/3-4-the-symmetric-group#theorem-3-4-6), the conjugacy classes of $S_4$ are given by cycle type: the identity, the six transpositions, the three double transpositions such as $(12)(34)$, the eight $3$-cycles and the six $4$-cycles. So $S_4$ has five irreducible representations, and the squares of their dimensions add up to $24$.

We know three of them. The rows of $U$ and $U'$ are the constant function $1$ and $\sgn$, and $\chi_V = (3, 1, -1, 0, -1)$ in the order of the table below. Since $$H(\chi_V, \chi_V) = \tfrac{1}{24}\bigl(9 + 6 \cdot 1 + 3 \cdot 1 + 8 \cdot 0 + 6 \cdot 1\bigr) = 1,$$ $V$ is irreducible. The twist $V' = V \otimes U'$ is irreducible with character $\chi_V\sgn = (3, -1, -1, 0, 1)$, and $V' \not\cong V$ because the characters differ at $(12)$. So far $1 + 1 + 9 + 9 = 20$, so the fifth irreducible representation $W$ has dimension $2$.

To find $\chi_W$, observe that $W \otimes U'$ is also a $2$-dimensional irreducible representation, and $W$ is the only one; so $W \otimes U' \cong W$ and $\chi_W\sgn = \chi_W$. Hence $\chi_W$ vanishes on the odd classes, those of $(12)$ and $(1234)$. Write $b = \chi_W((12)(34))$ and $a = \chi_W((123))$. Orthogonality to $\chi_U$ and to $\chi_V$ gives $$H(\chi_U, \chi_W) = \tfrac{1}{24}(2 + 3b + 8a) = 0, \qquad H(\chi_V, \chi_W) = \tfrac{1}{24}(6 - 3b) = 0,$$ so $b = 2$ and $a = -1$. The table is complete:

As a check, $H(\chi_W, \chi_W) = \frac{1}{24}(4 + 3 \cdot 4 + 8 \cdot 1) = 1$.

## <span class="num">14.1.1</span> Identifying $W$

The value $\chi_W((12)(34)) = 2$ tells us a great deal. The operator by which $(12)(34)$ acts on $W$ has order dividing $2$, so it is diagonalizable with eigenvalues $\pm 1$ (Lemma [13.1.5](/notes/math-55a/13-1-representations-and-subrepresentations#lemma-13-1-5)), and two such eigenvalues add up to $2$ only if both are $1$. So $(12)(34)$ acts on $W$ as the identity, and so do the other two double transpositions, which have the same character value. Hence the subgroup $$K = \{e,\ (12)(34),\ (13)(24),\ (14)(23)\} \cong \ZZ/2 \times \ZZ/2$$ lies in the kernel of $S_4 \to \GL(W)$. It is normal, being the union of the conjugacy classes of $e$ and of $(12)(34)$ (Proposition [3.2.13](/notes/math-55a/3-2-group-actions#proposition-3-2-13)), so this homomorphism factors through $S_4/K$ (Theorem [3.3.2](/notes/math-55a/3-3-the-isomorphism-theorems#theorem-3-3-2)).

To identify $S_4/K$, let $S_4$ act on the three ways of splitting $\{1, 2, 3, 4\}$ into two pairs, $$P_1 = \{12 \mid 34\}, \qquad P_2 = \{13 \mid 24\}, \qquad P_3 = \{14 \mid 23\}.$$ This gives a homomorphism $q : S_4 \to S_3$. Each double transposition preserves all three splittings, so $K \subseteq \ker q$. The transposition $(12)$ fixes $P_1$ and swaps $P_2$ and $P_3$, and $(123)$ permutes $P_1 \to P_3 \to P_2 \to P_1$, so the image of $q$ contains elements of orders $2$ and $3$, and $q$ is surjective. Then $|\ker q| = 24/6 = 4$, so $\ker q = K$, and $S_4/K \cong S_3$ by the First Isomorphism Theorem (Theorem [3.3.3](/notes/math-55a/3-3-the-isomorphism-theorems#theorem-3-3-3)). Under $q$, transpositions and $4$-cycles go to transpositions (for instance, $(1234)$ fixes $P_2$ and swaps $P_1$ and $P_3$), and $3$-cycles go to $3$-cycles.

Now let $W_0$ be the standard representation of $S_3$, regarded as a representation of $S_4$ in which $g$ acts as $q(g)$ does. Its character is $\chi_{W_0}(g) = \chi_{V_{S_3}}(q(g))$, where $V_{S_3}$ is the standard representation of $S_3$; by Example [13.4.5](/notes/math-55a/13-4-characters#example-13-4-5) this is $(2, 0, 2, -1, 0)$, which is $\chi_W$. So $W \cong W_0$ (Corollary [13.5.6](/notes/math-55a/13-5-orthogonality-of-characters#corollary-13-5-6)): $W$ is the standard representation of $S_3$, pulled back to $S_4$ along $S_4 \to S_4/K \cong S_3$.

## <span class="num">14.1.2</span> A Second Construction of $W$

We can also find $W$ inside $V \otimes V$. Its character is $\chi_V^2 = (9, 1, 1, 0, 1)$, and $$\begin{aligned}
H(\chi_U, \chi_V^2) &= \tfrac{1}{24}(9 + 6 + 3 + 0 + 6) = 1, \\
H(\chi_{U'}, \chi_V^2) &= \tfrac{1}{24}(9 - 6 + 3 + 0 - 6) = 0, \\
H(\chi_V, \chi_V^2) &= \tfrac{1}{24}(27 + 6 - 3 + 0 - 6) = 1, \\
H(\chi_{V'}, \chi_V^2) &= \tfrac{1}{24}(27 - 6 - 3 + 0 + 6) = 1.
\end{aligned}$$ So $V \otimes V$ contains $U \oplus V \oplus V'$, of dimension $7$, and the remaining summand has dimension $2$ and contains none of $U, U', V, V'$; it must be $W$. Thus $$V \otimes V \cong U \oplus V \oplus V' \oplus W,$$ and $\chi_W = \chi_V^2 - \chi_U - \chi_V - \chi_{V'}$, which again gives $(2, 0, 2, -1, 0)$. (Consistently, $H(\chi_V^2, \chi_V^2) = \frac{1}{24}(81 + 6 + 3 + 0 + 6) = 4$, the value for four non-isomorphic summands.)
